title: Paul's Missionary Trials
overview: Acts Chapter 14 recounts a pivotal segment of Paul and Barnabas’s first missionary journey, highlighting both the expansion of the gospel and the opposition it faced. The chapter details their bold preaching in Iconium, the miraculous healing in Lystra, and the resulting confusion of the people who mistake them for gods. Despite severe persecution, including Paul being stoned and left for dead, the apostles persist in preaching and strengthening new believers. This chapter illustrates the challenges of early Christian evangelism, the power of God working through signs and wonders, and the call to faithfulness amid suffering. It underscores the opening of the gospel to Gentiles and the establishment of church leadership, marking a foundational moment in the spread of Christianity.
structure:
**Verses 1-5: Bold Preaching and Division in Iconium.** Paul and Barnabas enter the synagogue, preaching so effectively that many Jews and Greeks believe, but unbelieving Jews stir opposition, causing division and attempts to stone the apostles.

**Verses 6-20: Ministry and Persecution in Lystra.** After fleeing Iconium, they preach in Lystra where Paul heals a crippled man, leading the crowd to mistake them for gods. The apostles reject this idolatry, urging repentance to the living God. Opposition returns, and Paul is stoned and left for dead but miraculously recovers.

**Verses 21-28: Strengthening the Churches and Return to Antioch.** Paul and Barnabas continue preaching in Derbe, then revisit previous cities to encourage disciples, appoint elders, and pray with fasting. They conclude their journey by returning to Antioch, reporting on God’s work among the Gentiles and remaining with the disciples for a time.

keyVerses.text: Long time therefore abode they speaking boldly in the Lord, which gave testimony unto the word of his grace, and granted signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the divine empowerment behind the apostles’ ministry, showing that their boldness and miraculous works authenticate the gospel message and demonstrate God's grace in action.

keyVerses.text: And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein :
keyVerses.significance: Paul and Barnabas firmly reject idolatry and redirect the people to the one true living God, emphasizing the Creator’s sovereignty and the call to repentance, central themes in Christian evangelism.

keyVerses.text: Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
keyVerses.significance: This verse teaches the necessity of perseverance through suffering for believers, connecting discipleship with enduring trials as a pathway to God’s kingdom.

keyVerses.text: And there came thither certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the people, and, having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead.
keyVerses.significance: The violent opposition Paul faces underscores the cost of gospel ministry and foreshadows the suffering all apostles would endure for Christ’s sake.

characters.name: Paul
characters.description: The primary apostle preaching the gospel, performing miracles, and enduring persecution. His leadership and boldness are central to the chapter’s narrative.

characters.name: Barnabas
characters.description: Paul’s companion and fellow missionary, known for encouragement and partnership in ministry. He is mistakenly identified as Jupiter by the Lystra crowd.

characters.name: Unbelieving Jews
characters.description: Opponents who stir up Gentiles against the apostles, inciting violence and opposition to the gospel message.

characters.name: The Lame Man
characters.description: A man crippled from birth who is miraculously healed by Paul, serving as a powerful testimony to God’s power and grace.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes that faithfulness to Christ often involves tribulation, as Paul and Barnabas face opposition yet continue their mission, reflecting the broader biblical call to endure hardship for the gospel.
Signs and wonders authenticate the apostles’ message, demonstrating God’s active presence and validating the gospel’s truth to both Jews and Gentiles.
Paul and Barnabas confront pagan worship, redirecting people from false gods to the living Creator, highlighting the biblical call to worship God alone.

themes.theme: Expansion of the Gospel to Gentiles
themes.description: The chapter shows the gospel breaking ethnic and cultural barriers, with Gentiles receiving faith and inclusion in God’s kingdom.

historicalContext: Acts 14 takes place during the early first century AD, within the Roman province of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). Cities like Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe were part of the Lycaonia region, characterized by a mix of Greek, Roman, and local pagan religious practices. Synagogues served as initial preaching venues for Jewish and God-fearing Gentiles. The political environment was Roman imperial rule, which allowed relative freedom for religious expression but also fostered tensions between Jewish communities and Gentiles. Pagan idolatry was widespread, and the local populations often interpreted miraculous events through their polytheistic worldview, as seen in the Lystra incident.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes God’s sovereign grace in empowering the apostles’ ministry and the necessity of persevering faith amid trials. The healing miracle is seen as a sign pointing to Christ’s power, and the rejection of idolatry underscores the call to worship God alone.

Dispensationalists highlight the transition from a primarily Jewish mission to the inclusion of Gentiles, viewing Acts 14 as a key moment in the church age where the gospel door is opened to all nations, accompanied by signs confirming the apostles’ authority.

Early church interpreters often saw Paul’s sufferings and miracles as typifying Christ’s own passion and resurrection power, encouraging believers to imitate apostolic endurance and faithfulness in the face of persecution.

crossReferences.connection: Paul’s statement about strength being made perfect in weakness parallels the perseverance through tribulation emphasized in Acts 14:22.
God’s invisible attributes and power are clearly seen in creation, echoing Paul’s appeal to the living God as Creator in Acts 14:15-17.
The call to remember those in prison and suffering aligns with the persecution Paul endures in this chapter.
The promise that believers will do greater works than Jesus connects to the signs and wonders performed by the apostles in Acts 14:3.
Paul’s appointment of elders in Acts 14:23 reflects the pastoral qualifications and church leadership instructions later outlined in Timothy.

application: Trust God’s power to work through your witness, even when facing opposition or discouragement.
Reject all forms of idolatry in your life and turn fully to the living God who created all things.
Encourage and strengthen fellow believers to remain steadfast in faith despite trials.
Recognize that suffering for Christ is part of the Christian journey and leads to spiritual maturity.
Pray fervently and seek God’s guidance in appointing and supporting church leaders.
Share the gospel boldly, relying on God’s grace to open hearts and confirm the message.
conclusion: Acts 14 powerfully illustrates the dynamic and often difficult reality of early Christian mission. Through bold preaching, miraculous signs, and steadfast endurance amid persecution, Paul and Barnabas advance the gospel into new regions and peoples. Their rejection of idolatry and commitment to strengthening new believers set a pattern for faithful ministry. This chapter challenges Christians today to trust God’s power, persevere through hardship, and actively participate in spreading the gospel, confident that God opens doors of faith and sustains His church.
timeline: c. AD 47-48 - Paul and Barnabas’s First Missionary Journey

definitions.definition: A Jewish place of worship and teaching where early Christians often began preaching the gospel.
Worthless or empty things; idols or false gods that cannot save or provide true life.
Spiritual leaders appointed in the early churches to shepherd and oversee the community of believers.
A region in Asia Minor where Lystra and Derbe were located, known for its pagan religious practices.

outline.heading: Preaching and Opposition in Iconium
outline.description: Paul and Barnabas preach boldly in the synagogue, resulting in many conversions but also fierce opposition that divides the city and leads to threats against their lives.

outline.heading: Miracles and Idolatry in Lystra
outline.description: After fleeing Iconium, the apostles heal a crippled man, prompting the crowd to mistake them for gods. They vehemently reject this worship and call the people to repentance.

outline.heading: Persecution and Recovery
outline.description: Paul is stoned by hostile Jews but miraculously survives, demonstrating God’s protection and the cost of gospel ministry.

outline.heading: Strengthening New Believers
outline.description: Paul and Barnabas continue preaching, teaching, and appointing elders in the churches they founded, encouraging believers to remain faithful despite trials.

outline.heading: Journey’s End and Report
outline.description: The missionaries travel through Pisidia and Pamphylia before returning to Antioch, where they report on God’s work among the Gentiles and stay with the disciples.
